topic: How Does the Internet Cross the Ocean?
angle: Over 99% of global internet traffic doesn't travel through space satellites, but through fragile glass strands no thicker than a garden hose resting on the ocean floor under miles of crushing pressure.
why: Explainer videos breaking down hidden infrastructure like Veritasium's fiber optics explainer (14.2M views) and underwater engineering marvels (19.6M views) prove massive global curiosity for unseen megastructures. The question is irresistible because almost everyone assumes internet data beams through wireless satellites, making the physical reality of cables under the ocean shocking yet tangible.

how do fiber optic cables work underwater
how deep are internet cables in the ocean
how internet travels across the world
facts: Over 95% to 99% of all intercontinental internet traffic travels through underwater submarine cables, not satellites.
There are over 550 active and planned commercial undersea fiber-optic cables worldwide, spanning approximately 1.4 million kilometers.
The core of an undersea cable contains optical fibers made of ultrapure silica glass, each scarcely thicker than a single human hair (about 125 to 250 microns).
Data travels through these glass strands as pulses of infrared light, bouncing internally without escaping through a physics principle called total internal reflection.
In deep open ocean (down to 8,000 meters), the cable is remarkably thin—typically only 17 to 20 millimeters in diameter, roughly the width of a standard garden hose.
Thick armored layers are only added near shorelines (shallow waters under 1,500 meters) to protect against commercial fishing trawlers and ship anchors.

The cross-section of a deep-sea cable consists of central glass fibers, petroleum jelly to block water penetration, a copper or aluminum power conductor, steel strength wires, and an outer protective polyethylene jacket.
Because light pulses degrade and lose intensity after roughly 60 to 100 kilometers, engineers splice in underwater repeaters (amplifiers) at regular intervals along the seafloor.
Underwater repeaters use Erbium-Doped Fiber Amplifiers (EDFA) to boost optical signals directly without converting light back into electrical data.
The copper tube inside the cable carries up to 10,000 volts of direct current (DC) across thousands of kilometers to power these submerged repeaters.
Specialized cable-laying ships carry thousands of miles of cable coiled in massive onboard tanks and slowly feed it into the ocean over voyages lasting weeks.
Near shorelines, unmanned underwater plows and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) jet high-pressure water to dig trenches 1 to 3 meters into the seabed to bury the cable.
In the deep ocean abyss, the cable is not buried; it simply rests directly on the ocean floor, guided carefully to avoid underwater mountains, trenches, and volcanic rifts.
Shark bites account for less than 1% of recorded cable damage; roughly 70% of cable cuts are caused by commercial fishing gear and dragged ship anchors.
When a cable snaps, monitoring stations pinpoint the break location within meters by firing light pulses and timing the optical reflection (Optical Time-Domain Reflectometry).

To fix a broken cable, repair ships lower specialized grapnel hooks to grab and sever the damaged section, winch both ends to a sterile cleanroom on deck, fusion-splice the glass fibers under microscopes, and lower the sealed joint back into the sea.
Underwater communications cables run through the Hormuz area.
Questions or concerns exist regarding who would face internet disruption if the undersea cables in Hormuz were severed.
